subject: Cognitive Science
title: Identity Formation
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Identity Formation.

hook.text: Goth one month, athlete the next. Teens try on identities like outfits. It's Erikson's identity crisis.

buildup.text: Erikson said adolescence is a struggle between identity and role confusion. You must find your self.

discovery.text: Marcia expanded this into four statuses: diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, and achievement.

twist.text: Foreclosure—committing without exploring—seems stable but often collapses under new experiences.

climax.text: Modern research extends identity formation into the twenties. Emerging adulthood is now recognized.

punchline.text: Finding yourself takes longer than expected.

quiz.question: What are Marcia's four identity statuses?

details.summary: Erik Erikson described adolescence as a period of identity crisis where individuals explore roles, values, and beliefs. James Marcia expanded this into four identity statuses: diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, and achievement. Identity formation continues well beyond adolescence into adulthood.
details.whyItMatters: Identity formation explains the turmoil and experimentation of adolescence. It is not pathology but a necessary developmental process that shapes lifelong self-concept.
takeaways: Erikson identified adolescence as the identity crisis period
Marcia defined four identity statuses from diffusion to achievement

faq.question: What are Marcia's four identity statuses?
faq.answer: Diffusion: no exploration or commitment. Foreclosure: commitment without exploration, adopting parents' values. Moratorium: active exploration without commitment. Achievement: exploration followed by commitment. Most adolescents move through several statuses before settling into achievement.

faq.question: Does identity formation end after adolescence?
faq.answer: No. Research shows identity can be reopened by major life events like career changes, parenthood, or cultural shifts. Adults revisit identity questions throughout life. Erikson himself described further identity work in his later life stages of intimacy, generativity, and integrity.
